sections.COMMENTS:
The Calabrian Arc is a narrow segment of mountain chain between the Tyrrhenian Sea (to the E) and the Ionian Sea (to the W). It stretches for 200 km between the Southern Apennines (to the N) and Sicily (to the SW).
The Calabrian Arc formed as a consequence of the subduction of oceanic crust under the southern margin of the European plate. The core of the Calabrian Arc itself is a remnant of that margin that includes crystalline units. Also sedimentary units coming from the northern margin of the African plate were progressively incorporated during the subduction process and contributed to form the present-day Calabrian Arc. The subduction of oceanic crust appears to be still active only in a narrow portion of the Calabrian Arc, near its southwestern end, between the Catanzaro Strait and the Messina Strait. To the north, although convergence is still active, the sedimentary cover of the African continental margin has been wedged into the Calabrian Arc and thrusted towards the foreland.
Seismic profiles across the Ionian Sea highlight the thrust structure of the eastern margin of the Calabrian Arc and of the submerged accretionary wedge that spans into the Ionian Sea for about 170 km. Seismic profiles and tomographic cross-sections also imaged the subduction slab underneath Calabria. On the contrary, most of the onshore portion of the Calabrian Arc is dominated by active extensional and strike-slip tectonics.
GPS velocity data show Europe â€“ Africa (Nubia) convergence of 3-5 mm/y across the trench of the Calabrian Arc (Dâ€™Agostino and Selvaggi, 2004; Devoti et al., 2008). GPS data also show extension across Calabria at about 3 mm/y (Serpelloni et al., 2005). Calabria is also characterized by the highest uplift rates in Italy (more than 1 mm/y; Bordoni and Valensise, 1998; Ferranti et al., 2006).
The seismicity of Calabria is both shallow and deep. Deep seismicity and tomography data depicts a well-developed subduction slab up to 500 km depth. Shallow seismicity is mainly extensional (Vannucci et al., 2004).
We propose that this Source is located on one of the main thrusts on the eastern side of the Calabrian Arc. The location corresponds to that part of the Calabrian Arc where the sedimentary cover of the African continental margin has been wedged into the chain and thrusted towards the foreland. The CROP M5 seismic line images a complex thrust structure called "Crotone structure", which corresponds to the southern portion of this Source. In this area, raised marine terraces testify to the rapid uplift that took place in Quaternary times (see Mauz and Hassler, 2000, among others).
On 8 March 1832 a M=6.5 earthquake took place at the southwestern end of this source. The geometry of the source is inferred from regional geological data, mainly seismic profiles (Van Dijk et al., 2000; Finetti, 2005). This source is assumed to operate by nearly pure thrusting.

pictures.t: Interpretation of the seismic profile CROP M-5

Geological map of the southern portion of the Crotone Peninsula. Five orders of marine terraces are recognized and their supposed age is indicated (from Zecchin et al. [2004]).
